summary: כֹּהֵן is the priest: the man Yahweh sets apart to draw near to him at his altar for the people, offering, making covering, waving the firstfruits before him, blowing the trumpets, and keeping and teaching his law (Exo 28:1; Num 18:7; Lev 23:10–11; Num 10:8; Mal 2:7). The office belonged by Yahweh’s gift to Aaron and his sons, and the stranger who came near died (Num 3:10; 18:7); the same word names Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, priests of Egypt, Midian and Baal, and the priests Jeroboam made from outside Levi. The verb (piel) is “serve as priest”, and כְּהֻנָּה is the priesthood, the office itself. The noun is the root’s first word; the same noun, priest, stands in Phoenician, Ugaritic, Aramaic and Ge’ez, and Arabic kāhin is the diviner.

senses.definition: One set apart by Yahweh to draw near to him and serve at his altar and within the veil on the people’s behalf: to offer what they bring, make covering for them, wave their firstfruits before him, blow the trumpets, carry the box of the covenant, and eat the holy things. doctrine.statement: The law kept king and priest apart: the priesthood was given to Aaron’s sons, and when king Uzziah went in to burn incense the priests withstood him and he was struck with leprosy (Num 18:7; 2Ch 26:16–21). Before the law Melchizedek was both king of Salem and priest to God Most High (Gen 14:18). Yahweh swears to the one he seats at his right hand, “You are a priest for ever after the manner of Melchizedek” (Psa 110:1, 4), and Zechariah says of the Branch who will build Yahweh’s temple, “he will sit and rule on his throne, and he will be a priest on his throne” (Zec 6:12–13). Hebrews applies Psa 110:4 to Christ, of Judah, a tribe of which Moses said nothing about priests; he is made priest by an oath and by the power of an endless life, not by descent (Heb 5:5–6; 7:13–17, 20–21); and “if he were on earth, he would not be a priest” while the law’s priests offered there (Heb 8:4). From the verses: the Messiah unites in himself the offices the law divided; his priesthood rests on Yahweh’s oath, and the throne on which he sits as priest is the throne on which he rules when he builds Yahweh’s temple.

The anointed priest could himself sin and bring the guilt of the people (Lev 4:3), and on the day of coverings Aaron first offered for himself and his house, then for the people (Lev 9:7; 16:6, 11, 15). Hebrews says that every high priest is taken from among men, is himself beset with weakness, and so must offer for himself as for the people (Heb 5:1–3); that Christ had to be made like his brothers in all things to be a merciful and faithful high priest, tempted in all points as we are, yet without sin (Heb 2:17; 4:15); that in the days of his flesh he prayed with strong crying to the one able to save him out of death and was heard (Heb 5:7); and that he does not need, as those high priests, to offer daily first for his own sins and then for the people’s, “for this he did once, when he offered up himself” (Heb 7:27). God brought him again from the dead by the blood of the everlasting covenant (Heb 13:20). From the verses: Christ is a high priest of our own nature, not of another; his one offering answers to both parts of the high priest’s work, for himself, who had no sin of his own but bore the nature that dies, and was saved out of death by his own blood, and for the people, whom he now saves to the uttermost (Heb 7:25).

Yahweh gave the priesthood to Aaron’s sons as “a service of gift”, and the stranger who came near died (Num 3:10; 18:7); Korah’s company, who sought the priesthood also, perished (Num 16:10, 31–35); Jeroboam, who made priests of whoever wished to fill his hand, sinned so that his house was cut off (1Ki 13:33–34); and Hosea says that a priest who rejects knowledge is rejected from serving as priest (Hos 4:6). Hebrews draws the rule: “no one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was”, and so Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest (Heb 5:4–5). From the verses: the right to draw near for others is never seized but given by God, and the one he gives it to must keep his knowledge.

At Sinai Yahweh promised Israel, if they obeyed his voice and kept his covenant, “you will be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exo 19:5–6). Isaiah says Zion’s restored people “will be called priests of Yahweh” and that Yahweh will take priests and Levites even from the nations gathered to him (Isa 61:6; 66:20–21). Peter gives Exo 19:6 to those who come to Christ, a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1Pe 2:5, 9); John says Christ has made them a kingdom and priests to God, who “will reign on the earth”, and that those in the first resurrection “will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with him a thousand years” (Rev 1:6; 5:10; 20:6). From the verses: the calling Israel received at Sinai is held now by those in Christ, and it is fulfilled when they are raised to reign with him on the earth.

Yahweh gave Phinehas “a covenant of a priesthood for ever” (Num 25:13) and spoke of his covenant of life and peace with Levi, on whose lips was the law of truth (Mal 2:4–7). Through Jeremiah he binds the Levitical priests to David’s throne: as surely as his covenant with day and night stands, David will not lack a son to reign on his throne nor the priests, the Levites, a man to offer before him (Jer 33:17–22). Malachi sees the Lord come suddenly to his temple and purify the sons of Levi, that they may offer to Yahweh in righteousness (Mal 3:1–4), and Ezekiel, shown a house still to be built, sees the priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept his charge when Israel went astray, draw near to serve him (Ezk 44:15). From the verses: the promise to the priests stands beside the promise to David’s son, and both look to the Lord’s coming to his temple.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Leviticus 23 (Lev 23:10, 11, 20) and Numbers 10 (Num 10:8). Root key כהנ is the corpus’s own. Left out, keys not claimed: כּוֹבַע “helmet” (k.as.af, 1Sa 17:5 etc.), filed under this root by alphabetical position only: it has no ה or נ, its by-form קוֹבַע (s.ap.am, 1Sa 17:38; Ezk 23:24) and the Aramaic, Syriac and Arabic qubbaʿa words point to a root qbʿ/kbʿ or a foreign word; and כּוּב (k.as.ae, Ezk 30:5), a gentilic people or land name, not a person, so no name entry. The verb is formed from the noun (piel only) and names no cognate of its own; it counts the noun’s through kin. Peshitta words: from SEDRA root CHN (lexemes 1474–1477); NT uses of the noun are 121, of which the passages cited are a sample; Hebrews uses ܟܘܡܪܐ (lexeme 1484) throughout instead. Greek: ἱερεύς is listed by the brief as a loan from Thayer’s “Hebr. כֹּהֵן”, which is an equivalent, not an etymology (ἱερεύς is from ἱερός), so it is recorded as a rendering. Open questions: (1) the sense “chief officer at the king’s side” rests on 2Sa 8:18 beside 1Ch 18:17 and on 1Ki 4:5; it could instead be read as David’s sons serving at the altar outside the law, which the text does not say. (2) The doctrine “high-priest-from-among-men” states the reading of Heb 7:27 in which Christ’s offering was for himself (his nature, not personal sin) as well as for the people: a judgment call for review. (3) “covenant-of-priesthood” leaves the form of the priests’ service in Ezekiel’s house unstated. (4) Ge’ez ካህን may be an Aramaic loan with Christianity; Dillmann and Leslau not consulted. Not consulted: CAL and DEAPS for Old and Imperial Aramaic khn (e.g. the Elephantine priests); Payne Smith for Syriac; DULAT for Ugaritic; the Arabic in Lane’s supplement; Mandaic kahna (Wiktionary only). No Akkadian cognate: Akkadian priests are šangû, ērib bīti and others; kânu “be firm” is kn, not khn, and is not followed.
